issues.explanation: 'People cycling' is hard to connect clinically to the rest of this rape-related profile. The other triggers, threats, appraisals, and strategies center on interpersonal closeness, malevolent intent, bodily vulnerability, and interpersonal hypervigilance; cycling stands out as a highly specific cue without support elsewhere in the formulation.

vignette:
At 77, Martha had spent most of her adult life working as an environmental scientist, the kind of person who knew how to move carefully through marshland, read a weather shift, and notice small changes in a landscape before anyone else did. She was single and had long been accustomed to managing on her own. The rape happened years ago during a period when she was still doing regular fieldwork. She had been out at an exposed research site, the sort of open terrain she once loved for its clarity and quiet. What remained most vivid to her was not only the assault itself but the moments around it: being isolated, realizing there was no one close enough to hear her, and feeling the terrible mismatch between the wide openness of the place and her inability to get to safety. A man was with her there, and afterward she came away with the conviction that being alone with a man could turn dangerous without warning. She had never felt that ordinary assumptions about professional trust could protect her again.

In the immediate aftermath, Martha tried to think her way back to some sense of order. She went over the day repeatedly, dwelling on how it could have been prevented. She told herself she should have stood differently, spoken differently, left earlier, noticed something in him sooner. The questions circled without resolution, but she returned to them constantly, as if one more pass through the details might produce a version of events in which she had kept herself safe. Alongside that was a deep shame about her body. What had happened to it felt degrading in a way she struggled to put into words, and she carried herself as though exposure itself were dangerous. She had come to believe that the event happened because of the way she acted, and this self-blame sat next to a broader certainty that you can never know who will harm you.

Over the months and years that followed, these beliefs showed up in the ordinary structure of her life. Physical affection became something she braced against. If a colleague or acquaintance moved in for a hug, even in a harmless social context, her whole body stiffened before she could explain it. Sexual situations or even the suggestion of intimacy felt intolerable, not because she was indifferent to companionship, but because closeness immediately placed her back in the logic of danger and shame. Being alone with men was especially difficult. In work settings she made practical adjustments that others might read as preference or habit: leaving office doors open, positioning herself near exits during meetings, declining rides, and arranging conversations in hallways rather than enclosed rooms whenever she could.

Her job still brought her into the kinds of settings she now found hardest to tolerate. As an environmental scientist, she was at times expected to inspect sites, attend field visits, or stand in open areas discussing land use and sampling plans. In open or exposed spaces she felt vulnerable in a way that was immediate and physical. She scanned the terrain automatically and could not settle until she had identified how she would leave if she needed to. That same calculation followed her indoors. Before she felt comfortable anywhere, she noted the exits and the fastest path to them. If someone nearby made a sudden movement, she went on guard at once, her attention snapping toward the motion before she knew who had moved or why. She avoided eye contact with people as a general rule, especially men, partly because looking directly at someone felt exposing and partly because she preferred to monitor the room without inviting interaction.

At home she lived as though interruption were always possible. She listened for sounds that might mean someone was entering the house and remained alert to small noises at night. She described herself as never fully off watch. Friends had gradually stopped trying to greet her warmly because she recoiled from hugs; some interpreted her reserve as aloofness. Professionally, she stayed competent, but coworkers noticed she was exacting about where meetings happened and reluctant to join site visits unless the arrangements felt tightly controlled. Martha understood these patterns as necessary. To her, they were not overreactions but sensible accommodations to a world in which danger could appear in an ordinary person, in a closed room, or in a sudden shift of someone’s body.

What finally brought her to seek help was not any single new event but the narrowing of her life. She was tired of organizing every day around distance, exits, and vigilance, and she felt the loneliness of having spent so long flinching from touch and avoiding closeness. Still, what frightened her most about treatment was the possibility of being asked to speak plainly about what had happened to her body, or of being encouraged to trust too quickly. At the same time, she hoped for something modest but profound: to enter a room without first plotting escape, to tolerate ordinary human warmth without feeling endangered, and to stop living as though harm were waiting just outside her line of sight.
